vulnerabilities.patternName: AMM Curve / Parameter Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.title: All internal DEX swaps hardcoded with zero minimum output (amountOutMin=0)
vulnerabilities.description: The _createTradeInfo function hardcodes tradeInfo.totalReceiveQuantity = 0, which is used as the minimum received amount for every DEX swap during both CKToken issuance and redemption. This value flows to _executeTrade where it is passed as _receiveQuantity (minToQuantity) to the exchange adapter's getTradeCalldata, meaning the actual on-chain DEX call (e.g., Uniswap swap) has amountOutMin=0. The subsequent _validatePostTrade check 'exchangedQuantity >= _tradeInfo.totalReceiveQuantity' becomes 'exchangedQuantity >= 0' which is always true for uint256, providing zero slippage protection. While user-facing functions accept _minCkTokenRec and _minRedeemTokenToRec as aggregate checks, individual component swaps execute with no per-swap protection, allowing sandwich attackers to extract value from each swap independently.

location.codeSnippet:
tradeInfo.totalReceiveQuantity = 0; // hardcoded zero min output
...
require(exchangedQuantity >= _tradeInfo.totalReceiveQuantity, "Slippage too big"); // always passes since 0

vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker monitors mempool for issueWithSingleToken2 or redeemToSingleToken transactions. 2. Attacker front-runs by buying the component token on the target DEX pool, pushing the price up. 3. User's transaction executes: _trade() calls _executeTrade with _receiveQuantity=0 as minToQuantity — the DEX swap completes at the manipulated price with no protection. 4. Attacker back-runs by selling the component token, capturing the price difference. 5. For multi-component CKTokens, this can be repeated for each component swap. 6. The aggregate _minCkTokenRec/_minRedeemTokenToRec may still pass if set loosely, or the user may set it to 0 out of convenience.
vulnerabilities.impact: Sandwich attackers can extract significant value from every swap during CKToken issuance and redemption. For a CKToken with N components, there are up to 2N vulnerable swap points (N during issue, N during redeem). The _dustToReturn function creates additional vulnerable swaps when converting excess component tokens back to the issue token. Estimated loss per transaction: 1-10% of trade value per swap depending on pool liquidity and sandwich attack sophistication.

matchedCases.matchReason: Same root cause: swaps executing with amountOutMin=0 allowing MEV bots to extract value via front-run and back-run

vulnerabilities.patternName: Oracle Address Update Without Timelock/Multi-sig
vulnerabilities.title: Pricing engine address can be instantly replaced by single owner without timelock
vulnerabilities.description: The changeTesseraEngine() function allows the tesseraOwner to unilaterally and instantly replace the TesseraEngine address, which is the sole price source for all swaps. There is no timelock delay, no multi-signature requirement, and no two-step transfer pattern. The TesseraEngine determines all swap amounts via swapAmount(), so a malicious or compromised owner can redirect all swap pricing to a manipulated engine, causing every subsequent swap to extract value from users. This is equivalent to replacing the oracle/price feed address with no guardrails.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises or IS the tesseraOwner key; 2. Deploy a malicious engine contract that returns manipulated swap amounts (e.g., returns less tokenOut than fair value, or more tokenIn than needed); 3. Call changeTesseraEngine() to swap the legitimate engine for the malicious one — takes effect immediately; 4. All subsequent user swaps route through the malicious engine, silently extracting value; 5. Optionally, change the engine back to cover tracks. No on-chain mechanism prevents or delays this.
vulnerabilities.impact: A compromised owner key enables instant theft of value from all users who have pending or future swap transactions. Users who have already approved the TesseraSwap contract for tokenIn would lose funds on every swap through manipulated pricing. Since there is no timelock, users have zero window to react or withdraw approvals.

matchedCases.matchReason: Single privileged key compromise enabled instant protocol takeover with no timelock or multi-sig barrier
Trusted parameter (root/engine) could be changed without adequate validation, affecting all downstream operations

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Treasury address and token rescue executable instantly by single owner without timelock
vulnerabilities.description: Both changeTesseraTreasury() and rescueTokens() allow the tesseraOwner to instantly redirect fund flows without any timelock or multi-sig protection. The treasury address is the source and destination of all swap tokens (tokenOut flows from treasury, tokenIn flows to treasury). A compromised owner can change the treasury to an attacker-controlled address, causing all incoming tokenIn from user swaps to be sent to the attacker. Additionally, rescueTokens() allows the owner to sweep ANY token held by the contract with no bounds.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises the tesseraOwner key; 2. Call changeTesseraTreasury() to set treasury to attacker address — instant effect; 3. Front-run user swap transactions: when tesseraSwapWithAllowances executes, IERC20(tokenIn).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, tesseraTreasury, amountIn) sends the user's input tokens directly to the attacker's address; 4. The attacker may or may not honor the tokenOut side, depending on whether they hold the output token. Even if they provide tokenOut, they capture all incoming tokenIn at manipulated rates. 5. Alternatively, use rescueTokens() to sweep any tokens temporarily held by the contract during callback swaps.
vulnerabilities.impact: A compromised owner can redirect all user swap inputs to an attacker-controlled treasury. Any user who has approved the TesseraSwap contract for their tokens is at risk of losing funds on the next swap. The rescueTokens function provides an additional vector to extract any tokens that accumulate in the contract.

matchedCases.matchReason: Privileged role could instantly change critical protocol parameters (fee/ treasury addresses) affecting user fund flows without timelock

vulnerabilities.patternName: AMM Curve / Parameter Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.title: Unprotected sync() function enables anyone to drain contract USDT into DEX pair and manipulate reserves
vulnerabilities.description: The sync() function is declared as 'external' with NO access control modifier (no onlyOwner, no onlyContractDealer). Any caller can trigger it at any time to transfer ALL USDT held by the Staking contract into the Uniswap V2 pair and then call pair.sync(), which force-updates the pair's tracked reserves. This (1) drains USDT that should be available for reward payouts, making the contract insolvent, and (2) directly manipulates the AMM's reserve ratio (K value), inflating token price. Since maxStakeAmount(), dailyLimit(), and the unstake swap path all depend on pair reserves, this manipulation cascades into all protocol operations.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Monitor the chain for USDT accumulation in the Staking contract (from staking deposits where internal swaps/liquidity additions leave residual USDT, or from reward distributions). 2. Call sync() to push all contract USDT into the pair as a unilateral donation. 3. pair.sync() updates reserves to include the donated USDT, changing K and inflating token price. 4. The contract can no longer fulfill unstake reward obligations (USDT is in the pair, not the contract). 5. All reserve-dependent calculations (maxStakeAmount, dailyLimit) are now based on manipulated reserves. 6. Repeat to continuously drain any incoming USDT.
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete drainage of contract USDT holdings, making all pending staking rewards unpayable. The pair's reserves are permanently manipulated, affecting every subsequent staking and unstaking operation. Users' funds are directly at risk as the contract becomes insolvent.

matchedCases.matchReason: Publicly callable sync() or skim() on pair reserves manipulation, same technique of donating tokens then syncing to change K value

vulnerabilities.patternName: AMM Curve / Parameter Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.title: Zero slippage protection (amountOutMin=0) in internal swap and addLiquidity enables sandwich attacks during staking
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTokenForToken() internal function hardcodes amountOutMin=0 when calling swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens. Similarly, _swapAndAddLiquidity() passes amountAMin=0 and amountBMin=0 to V2Router.addLiquidity(). These are contract-internal automated swaps triggered during user staking operations. Since there is no contract-enforced minimum output, MEV bots can sandwich-attack every staking transaction: front-running to move the pair price, letting the staker's swap execute at a worse rate, then back-running to capture the profit. The LP tokens from addLiquidity are sent to address(0) (permanently locked), so the user loses value irrecoverably.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. MEV bot detects a pending stake() transaction in the mempool. 2. Bot front-runs by selling a large amount of tokens into the pair, crashing the token price. 3. The stake() transaction executes _swapAndAddLiquidity: the internal swap buys tokens at the depressed price (getting fewer tokens due to amountOutMin=0), and liquidity is added at the manipulated ratio. 4. LP tokens go to address(0) — permanently locked at the bad ratio. 5. Bot back-runs by buying tokens back at the restored price, capturing the difference. 6. The staker receives fewer staking shares (minted based on the smaller 'got' amount) and loses value permanently.
vulnerabilities.impact: Every staking transaction can be sandwiched, causing users to receive fewer tokens from the internal swap and worse LP ratios. Over time, this systematically extracts value from stakers. With high-frequency staking, cumulative losses can be substantial.

matchedCases.caseName: Common MEV sandwich attacks on tokens with auto-liquidity
matchedCases.matchReason: Identical pattern: contract performs internal swaps with amountOutMin=0 during token operations, enabling sandwich extraction

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Hardcoded backdoor address in _checkOwner bypasses ownership, granting unbounded control over all economic parameters and fund withdrawals
vulnerabilities.description: The _checkOwner() function in the modified Ownable contract contains a hardcoded address (0xE746c9043Aa0106853c5e4380A9A307Fe385378e) that bypasses the standard ownership check. This address can call ALL onlyOwner functions across both Staking and IConf contracts without being the actual owner. All economic parameters (validAmount, reserveURate, dayInRate, payRates, stakeDays, levelKpiThresholds) can be modified instantly without timelock or bounds. The backdoor holder can also withdraw any token via withdrawalTokens() and any ETH via withdrawalETH(), create fake stakes via stakeOwner(), and force-unstake any user's position via unstakeOwner().

Calls setUint(3, 0) to set dayInRate to 0, blocking all new staking. 3. Calls withdrawalTokens(_USDT, attacker, balance) to drain all USDT. 4. Calls withdrawalTokens(conf.token(), attacker, balance) to drain all tokens. 5. Calls setUint(1, 0) to set validAmount to 0, disrupting all level calculations. 6. vulnerabilities.patternName: Spot Price Directly Used as Pricing Basis
vulnerabilities.title: Staking capacity limits (maxStakeAmount, dailyLimit) calculated from spot pair USDT balance without TWAP, enabling flash loan manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The maxStakeAmount() function reads USDT.balanceOf(IToken(conf.token()).V2Pair()) directly to calculate the maximum stake size as a percentage of current pool reserves. Similarly, _updateDailyIn() and dailyLimit() use the same spot balance to compute daily staking caps. Since these are instantaneous readings without any time-weighted averaging, an attacker can use a flash loan to temporarily inflate the pair's USDT balance, causing maxStakeAmount() and dailyLimit() to return artificially high values, then stake a large amount before the reserves normalize.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker flash-loans a large amount of USDT. 2. Swaps it into the pair (or directly transfers USDT to the pair and calls sync()), temporarily inflating the pair's USDT balance. 3. Calls stake() with an amount up to the inflated maxStakeAmount() — bypassing the intended capacity limit. 4. The staking operation processes at the manipulated capacity, allowing the attacker to stake far more than intended. 5. When the flash loan is repaid and reserves normalize, the attacker has locked in a larger staking position than the protocol intended to allow. 6. This can be combined with the public sync() vulnerability for amplified impact.
vulnerabilities.impact: Attackers can bypass staking capacity limits to stake arbitrarily large amounts, gaining disproportionate staking rewards and team KPI credit. This dilutes other stakers' relative positions and can be used to game the referral/level reward system.

matchedCases.caseName: Flash loan reserve manipulation attacks on capacity-limited protocols
matchedCases.matchReason: Same technique: flash loan to inflate pool reserves, bypassing capacity checks that read spot balances

vulnerabilities.patternName: Spot Price Directly Used as Pricing Basis
vulnerabilities.title: totalAssets() uses spot pool tick for valuation when twapWindowSeconds == 0 (default state)
vulnerabilities.description: The totalAssets() function reads the spot tick directly from pool.slot0() when twapWindowSeconds == 0. Since twapWindowSeconds is never set in initialize(), the contract defaults to spot pricing mode from deployment. This tick is used by VaultMathLib.getQuoteAtTick() to convert non-asset token balances (e.g., WETH) into asset value (e.g., USDC). Since totalAssets() feeds into convertToShares() and convertToAssets(), the vault's entire share exchange rate is derived from this manipulatable spot price. An attacker can flash-loan tokens, swap in the same Uniswap V3 pool to move the tick, and exploit the inflated/deflated valuation for deposit/redeem arbitrage within a single transaction.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker deposits $100K USDC into the vault, receiving shares based on totalAssets() at the current (fair) pool tick. 2. In the same transaction, attacker flash-loans ~$10M USDC from Aave V3 (available on Base) and swaps it into the Uniswap V3 pool, pushing the tick up significantly (e.g., WETH price +30-50%). 3. totalAssets() now overvalues the vault's non-asset token holdings by the manipulated ratio. 4. Attacker calls redeem() on their shares — convertToAssets() returns a higher USDC amount because totalAssets() is inflated. 5. The vault pays out from idle balances and strategy LP withdrawal (which at the manipulated tick returns mostly USDC). 6. Attacker repays the flash loan. Net profit = (inflated redemption - original deposit - flash loan fee). On a $1M TVL vault with ~50% non-asset exposure, a 30% price manipulation yields ~$15K profit per $100K deposit cycle.
vulnerabilities.impact: Direct theft of user funds. Every depositor's share value is determined by a spot price that can be manipulated in a single transaction via flash loan. The attacker extracts value from honest depositors by redeeming at an inflated exchange rate. This affects ALL deposits and redemptions while twapWindowSeconds remains 0.

matchedCases.matchReason: Same single-transaction spot price manipulation via flash loan to exploit protocol valuation
ERC4626 vault share pricing manipulated via spot AMM price oracle

vulnerabilities.patternName: Short-Window / Manipulatable TWAP
vulnerabilities.title: No minimum bound on TWAP window and silent fallback to spot price on observe() failure
vulnerabilities.description: Even when twapWindowSeconds > 0, two issues remain: (1) setTwapWindowSeconds() and setAllParams() accept ANY positive value with no minimum — an admin (or compromised keeper) can set it to 1 second, making the TWAP essentially a spot price vulnerable to multi-block MEV manipulation. (2) _consultTwap() catches any revert from pool.observe() and silently falls back to slot0() spot tick. If the pool has insufficient observation cardinality (common for new or low-traffic pools), observe() reverts and the TWAP protection is bypassed entirely without any warning. This means even with TWAP 'enabled', the vault may operate on spot pricing.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: Scenario A (short window): Admin sets twapWindowSeconds = 10. Attacker executes a two-block attack: Block 1 — flash swap to move price; Block 2 — deposit/redeem at manipulated TWAP (10-second window is trivially manipulable). Scenario B (cardinality fallback): Keeper sets pool to a newly created Uniswap V3 pool with default observation cardinality (which may only store ~10 minutes of data). If twapWindowSeconds exceeds available observations, observe() reverts, _consultTwap falls back to spot tick, and the vault is fully vulnerable to single-transaction flash loan manipulation.
vulnerabilities.impact: TWAP protection can be trivially bypassed or degraded to spot pricing, re-enabling the VULN-001 attack vector even when the admin believes TWAP is active. A compromised keeper setting pool to a low-cardinality pool enables silent degradation.

matchedCases.matchReason: TWAP mechanism silently degraded to spot pricing, enabling manipulation

vulnerabilities.recommendation: 1. Enforce minimum 1800 seconds (30 min) in all TWAP window setters. 2. In _consultTwap(), revert instead of falling back to spot price when observe() fails: `} catch { revert InvalidParams(); }`. 3. Before setting a new pool in setStrategyParams(), verify the pool has sufficient observation cardinality by calling `IUniswapV3Pool(pool).increaseObservationCardinalityNext(requiredSlots)` or checking via observe(). 4. Add a health check that reverts totalAssets() if the TWAP window cannot be satisfied.

vulnerabilities.patternName: AMM Curve / Parameter Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.title: Redeem fallback path withdraws LP with hardcoded zero slippage minimums
vulnerabilities.description: In the redeem() function, when the primary strategy withdrawal fails (e.g., due to slippage check), the catch block calls _withdrawFromStrategyInternal(liq, 0, 0), passing amount0Min=0 and amount1Min=0 to the strategy's withdrawToVault(). This means the fallback LP withdrawal accepts ANY token amounts regardless of the current pool price. A sandwich attacker can exploit this by front-running the redeem transaction with a pool-manipulating swap, causing the primary withdrawal to fail (minimums not met), then the fallback executes with zero protection, and the attacker back-runs to extract the price difference.

location.codeSnippet:
try IStrategyUniswapV3(strategy).withdrawToVault(liq, m0, m1) returns (uint256, uint256) {}
catch { _withdrawFromStrategyInternal(liq, 0, 0); }

vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker monitors mempool for a large redeem() transaction. 2. Attacker front-runs with a large swap in the vault's pool, moving the tick significantly (e.g., pushing it to the edge of the LP position's range). 3. The primary withdrawToVault(liq, m0, m1) reverts because the actual returned amounts are below the computed minimums (m0, m1). 4. The catch block executes _withdrawFromStrategyInternal(liq, 0, 0), which succeeds but returns a heavily skewed token ratio (mostly the depreciated token). 5. Attacker back-runs with a reverse swap to capture the price difference. 6. The redeemer receives fewer total value tokens than they should have. Profit scales with LP position size and price manipulation depth.
vulnerabilities.impact: Users redeeming shares can lose a significant portion of their withdrawal value to sandwich attackers when the primary withdrawal path fails. The loss is bounded by the pool's liquidity depth and the LP position's range, but for concentrated positions near the current tick, losses can exceed 10-20% of the withdrawal value.

matchedCases.caseName: Various Uniswap V3 LP Sandwich Attacks
matchedCases.matchReason: Zero-slippage-tolerance LP withdrawal exploited via sandwich attack on concentrated liquidity position

vulnerabilities.patternName: Spot Price Directly Used as Pricing Basis
vulnerabilities.title: Flash-loan manipulatable spot reserves used for profit fee calculation and tOwnedU tracking
vulnerabilities.description: The _transfer function reads instantaneous spot reserves from IUniswapV2Pair.getReserves() in both the buy and sell paths to calculate tOwnedU (user's USDT-equivalent purchase cost) and profit-based fees. There is no TWAP, cumulative price, or any time-weighted averaging mechanism applied. The profit fee system compares amountUOut (calculated from current spot reserves) against tOwnedU to determine whether a user has 'profit.' An attacker can manipulate the pool reserves via flash loan or multi-transaction sandwich to suppress the perceived amountUOut, causing it to fall below tOwnedU, thereby evading the 25% profit fee entirely. Additionally, deliveryReserveU() is a public function that anyone can call to overwrite _dailyCloseReserveU with the current spot reserve, meaning external contracts relying on getReserveU() would receive a manipulated value.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker buys ATM tokens at price P, establishing tOwnedU = X; 2. Token price rises naturally to 2P; 3. Attacker sells a large number of tokens (from a secondary wallet or via flash swap) into the pool, crashing the spot price below P; 4. Attacker immediately sells their profitable position — spot reserves now show amountUOut < tOwnedU, so no profit fee is charged (saves 25% of profit); 5. Attacker buys back the dumped tokens at the artificially low price, recovering their position while the price normalizes; 6. Net result: attacker evaded profit fees that should have been distributed to marketing/dividend/staking. The public deliveryReserveU() function also allows an attacker to poison _dailyCloseReserveU by calling it immediately after manipulating the pool.
vulnerabilities.impact: Attacker can evade the 25% profit fee on profitable sells by manipulating spot reserves before selling. This directly reduces protocol revenue (marketing and dividend funds) and creates unfair fee distribution. The attack is most profitable in low-liquidity pools where manipulation cost is low relative to fee savings. External contracts using getReserveU() for pricing (e.g., staking rewards) would also receive manipulated values.

matchedCases.matchReason: Same technique of using flash-loan-manipulated spot reserves for on-chain pricing decisions without TWAP protection
Spot-price-based profit/fee calculation manipulated via reserve manipulation

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Replace spot reserve readings with a Uniswap V2 TWAP oracle (observation over >=30 minute window) for profit calculation. Use price1CumulativeLast / price0CumulativeLast with block timestamps to compute time-weighted average price. Additionally, restrict deliveryReserveU() to onlyOwner or authorized callers to prevent public manipulation of daily close reserves.

vulnerabilities.patternName: AMM Curve / Parameter Misconfiguration
vulnerabilities.title: Contract-internal fee swap hardcodes amountOutMin=0 enabling sandwich extraction
vulnerabilities.description: The _swapTokenForUsdt function, which is called internally by _swapTokenForFund during sell transactions, hardcodes amountOutMin to 0 when calling uniswapV2Router.swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens. This means the contract accepts ANY output amount from the token-to-USDT swap, providing zero slippage protection. Since this swap converts accumulated fee tokens (up to swapAtAmount = 200 ATM tokens) to USDT for distribution to marketing and dividend addresses, a MEV sandwich attacker can front-run the swap by dumping ATM tokens to depress the price, let the contract swap at the artificially low price, then buy back ATM tokens — extracting value from the protocol's fee revenue.

location.codeSnippet:
uniswapV2Router.swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens(
    tokenAmount,
    0, // accept any amount of ETH
    path,
    to,
    block.timestamp
);

vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. MEV bot monitors the mempool for sell transactions where contractTokenBalance > swapAtAmount (200 ATM); 2. Bot front-runs with a large ATM→USDT swap, depressing the ATM price; 3. The contract's _swapTokenForFund executes with amountOutMin=0, swapping fee tokens at the manipulated low price — receiving minimal USDT; 4. Bot back-runs with a USDT→ATM buy, recovering tokens at the low price; 5. Net result: the protocol's marketing and dividend addresses receive significantly less USDT than fair market value. This can be repeated on every sell that triggers the swap threshold.
vulnerabilities.impact: Each time _swapTokenForFund is triggered, a sandwich attacker can extract a significant portion of the swap value. With swapAtAmount=200 ATM and frequent trading, this results in continuous revenue drain from the protocol's fee distribution mechanism. The loss per sandwich depends on pool liquidity and swap size but can easily exceed $1000 per attack in active trading conditions.

matchedCases.matchReason: Identical pattern: tax token contracts with internal swap-back logic using amountOutMin=0 being sandwiched by MEV bots

vulnerabilities.recommendation:
Calculate a minimum output amount using a TWAP oracle or spot price with a reasonable slippage tolerance (e.g., 5-10%). Example fix:
```solidity
uint256 expectedOut = getExpectedUsdtOut(tokenAmount); // from TWAP
uint256 minOut = (expectedOut * 90) / 100; // 10% slippage tolerance
uniswapV2Router.swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens(
    tokenAmount,
    minOut,
    path,
    to,
    block.timestamp
);
```

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Owner can unilaterally change critical economic parameters without timelock or bounds
vulnerabilities.description: Multiple functions allow the owner to immediately change critical economic parameters without any timelock, multi-sig, or governance process. setNumTokensSellRate can set the swap-back rate up to 100%, setSwapAtAmount can trigger swaps on any threshold (even 1 wei), setColdTime can disable sell cooldowns or freeze sells indefinitely, and setMarketingAddress/setDividendAddress can redirect fee revenue to any address. These changes take effect immediately and affect all existing positions. Combined with the CL-03 vulnerability, setting numTokensSellRate to 100% and swapAtAmount to a low value would maximize sandwich attack exposure for all users.

Every sell transaction now triggers a full balance swap-back with amountOutMin=0 (amplifying CL-03); 3. Owner sets marketingAddress and dividendAddress to their own wallets, redirecting all fee revenue; 4. Owner can set coldTime to type(uint40).max, effectively freezing all sells; 5. All changes take effect immediately with no window for users to react or withdraw.
vulnerabilities.impact: A compromised or malicious owner can drain protocol revenue by redirecting fee addresses, amplify MEV extraction by adjusting swap parameters, or freeze user sells by setting an extreme coldTime. Users have no time to react due to the absence of timelock. This represents a direct fund loss risk for all token holders.

matchedCases.matchReason: Same pattern of owner controlling fee rates, swap thresholds, and fee recipient addresses without timelock, enabling immediate fund redirection

vulnerabilities.patternName: Spot Price Directly Used as Pricing Basis
vulnerabilities.title: Flash-loan manipulatable spot AMM price drives dynamic sell tax, enabling fund extraction via griefing
vulnerabilities.description: The contract reads spot AMM reserves via getCurrentPrice() → getReserves() without any TWAP or oracle aggregation. This spot price feeds into getTokenPriceUsdt(), which is called in _update() during every non-exempt transfer to populate an hourly price ring buffer (updateHourlyLow). When users sell OLPC to the swap pair, percentChangeFrom24hLowest() compares the 24h lowest stored price against the earliest hour's start price. If the lowest is below startPrice (position==1), an additional tax of up to (value * percent * 2) / 10000 is applied — capped at 90% of the sell amount on top of the 10% base sell tax. An attacker can flash-loan or use capital to dump LABUBU into the OLPC/LABUBU pair, artificially crashing the OLPC spot price. A subsequent trivial OLPC transfer records this manipulated low in the ring buffer. For up to 24 hours afterward, ALL legitimate sellers face near-100% total tax (10% base + up to 90% additional), losing their entire sell amount to burns and node distributions. The attacker profits from supply reduction if they hold OLPC, or can buy at the crashed price after unwinding their manipulation.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker flash-loans a large amount of LABUBU tokens. 2. Sells LABUBU into the OLPC/LABUBU PancakeSwap pair, crashing OLPC's spot price by 90%+. 3. Performs a trivial OLPC transfer (e.g., 1 wei to a non-exempt address) which triggers _update() → getTokenPriceUsdt() → updateHourlyLow(), recording the manipulated low price in the ring buffer. 4. Unwinds the flash loan (buys back LABUBU at approximately the original price). 5. For the next 24 hours, any legitimate OLPC seller faces percentChangeFrom24hLowest() returning position=1 with pctScaled ≈ 9000, resulting in taxAmount2 = (value * 9000 * 2) / 10000 = 1.8×value, capped at 0.9×value. Combined with the 10% base tax, sellers lose 100% of their tokens to burn/nodeAddress. 6. Attacker benefits from supply reduction (burned tokens) if holding OLPC, or acquires OLPC cheaply from trapped sellers.
vulnerabilities.impact: All OLPC holders attempting to sell within 24 hours of manipulation lose up to 100% of their tokens to tax. This effectively traps user funds and can be repeated every 24 hours at minimal cost (gas + swap fees). The attack requires only flash-loanable capital and costs approximately $10-50 in gas/fees, while affecting the entire holder base.

matchedCases.matchReason: Flash loan used to manipulate spot AMM price which was then used as oracle input for economic decisions
Spot price from AMM reserves used as pricing basis without TWAP, manipulated via flash loan in single transaction

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Replace spot price with a robust TWAP oracle. Use PancakeSwap's cumulative price observations with a minimum 30-minute window. Additionally, cap the maximum additional sell tax at a reasonable percentage (e.g., 20%) regardless of price drop magnitude. Example fix: use Uniswap V3 TWAP or Chainlink price feed for getTokenPriceUsdt(), and change the tax formula to: uint256 taxAmount2 = (value * percent) / (BASE_PERCENT * 5); // cap additional tax at 20%

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: updateData() has no access control — anyone can set deflationRate and dropRate from external contract
vulnerabilities.description: The updateData() function is declared as external with NO access control modifier (no onlyOwner, no onlyAuthorized). It reads distributeRate, deflationRate, and dropRate from ISwapPool(tokenAddress).getDistributeRate() and directly assigns deflationRate and dropRate to whatever values the external contract returns. While tokenAddress defaults to address(0) (making the call revert), once the owner sets tokenAddress via setTokenAddress(), ANY caller can invoke updateData() to overwrite deflationRate and dropRate with arbitrary values from the external contract. The deflationRate is critically used in burnSwap() to determine what fraction of the LP pair's tokens are burned/distributed: balance = (balance * deflationRate) / BASE_PERCENT. If deflationRate is set to 10000 (100%), the entire pair balance becomes subject to burn/distribution. Additionally, distributeRate can only ratchet upward (never decrease), meaning repeated calls permanently inflate it.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Owner sets tokenAddress to a SwapPool contract (legitimate setup step). 2. If the SwapPool contract is compromised, has a bug, or can be influenced by an attacker, the attacker calls updateData(). 3. The attacker-controlled getDistributeRate() returns deflationRate_ = 10000 and distributeRate_ = 9000. 4. distributeRate is permanently set to 9000 (cannot decrease). 5. When burnSwap() is next called (if isBurnSwapPair is enabled), 100% of the pair's OLPC balance is processed, with 90% going to distributorAddress. This drains LP liquidity.
vulnerabilities.impact: If the external SwapPool contract returns malicious values (due to compromise, bug, or manipulation), an attacker can drain LP pair liquidity via burnSwap() and permanently inflate distributeRate. The lack of bounds checking on deflationRate (can be 0 to 10000+) and the upward-only ratchet on distributeRate compound the risk.

matchedCases.caseName: Various rug pulls via unprotected setter functions
matchedCases.matchReason: Economic parameters modifiable without access control, enabling fund extraction through authorized mechanisms

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add onlyOwner or a dedicated role modifier to updateData(). Add bounds checking: require(deflationRate_ <= 1000, 'deflation too high'); require(dropRate_ <= 1000, 'drop too high'). Allow distributeRate to decrease as well, or add a maximum cap. Example: function updateData() external onlyOwner { ... require(deflationRate_ <= MAX_DEFLATION_RATE, 'exceeds bound'); ... }

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Owner can set decimalsValue without bounds, controlling 100% buy-side token burn (honeypot risk)
vulnerabilities.description: The setDecimalsValue() function allows the owner to set decimalsValue to any uint128 without upper or lower bounds. This value is used in the _update() override for buy transactions (from swapPair): super._update(from, BURN_ADDRESS, value * decimalsValue); value = 0. When decimalsValue = 1 (current default), 100% of tokens purchased from the AMM pair are burned and the buyer receives nothing. When decimalsValue = 0, buyers receive tokens normally. The owner can toggle this at will without timelock, creating a honeypot scenario where users buy tokens (paying real value) but receive nothing. Additionally, if decimalsValue > 1, the multiplication value * decimalsValue will overflow for large purchases (Solidity 0.8+ reverts), effectively blocking all buys above a tiny threshold.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Owner deploys contract with decimalsValue = 0 (allows buying). 2. Users buy OLPC tokens from PancakeSwap, paying LABUBU/BNB. 3. Owner calls setDecimalsValue(1), enabling 100% buy-side burn. 4. New buyers continue purchasing through PancakeSwap router (which interacts with the pair), but all purchased tokens are instantly burned — buyers receive nothing. 5. The LABUBU/BNB paid by buyers remains in the pair, benefiting LP holders (including owner). 6. Owner can toggle back to 0 to sell their own accumulated tokens, then re-enable the burn trap.
vulnerabilities.impact: Buyers can be trapped into paying for tokens they never receive. The owner has unilateral, immediate (no timelock) control over whether buying is functional or confiscatory. This is a classic honeypot pattern that can extract user funds.

matchedCases.matchReason: Owner-controlled buy/sell tax that can be set to 100%, confiscating buyer funds without timelock

vulnerabilities.recommendation: If the buy-burn mechanism is intentional, enforce immutability or governance control: make decimalsValue immutable after initialization, or require a 48-hour timelock before changes take effect. At minimum, add bounds: require(decimalsValue_ <= 1, 'exceeds max'); and emit an event for monitoring. Better yet, remove the dynamic buy-burn entirely and use a fixed, transparent tax rate.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Admin can change presale price without timelock or bounds
vulnerabilities.description: The setPrice() function allows the owner to instantly change the token exchange rate to any positive value without timelock delay, upper/lower bounds, or governance approval. This directly affects all buy() and sell() operations. A compromised or malicious admin could lower the price to near-zero before users sell (causing them to receive negligible USDT), or raise the price to inflate token amounts for selected buyers. The ownership transfer mechanism has a 48h timelock, but parameter changes by the current owner take effect immediately.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises admin key (or insider is malicious); 2. Calls setPrice(1) to set price to near-zero; 3. Users who try to sell tokens now receive negligible USDT (usdtAmount = amount * 1 / 1e18 ≈ 0); 4. Alternatively, raise price then use sell() to drain contract USDT at inflated rates; 5. All existing contributor expectations are invalidated instantly with no warning period
vulnerabilities.impact: Users who contributed USDT and hold AIS tokens can have their sell-back value reduced to near-zero. The contract's entire economic mechanism (buy price, sell-back guarantee) can be subverted in a single transaction.

matchedCases.matchReason: Admin changed presale parameters without timelock to disadvantage users

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add a timelock to price changes and enforce bounds: `require(_price >= MIN_PRICE && _price <= MAX_PRICE, 'out of bounds');` Additionally, consider requiring 24h notice before price changes take effect, allowing users to react.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: rescueToken allows admin to drain all AIS tokens and USDT without timelock
vulnerabilities.description: The rescueToken() function allows the owner to withdraw ANY token from the contract, including the AIS tokens deposited for user claims and all USDT raised. Combined with withdrawToTreasury(), the admin can completely drain the contract in a single transaction. This means all user contributions and unclaimed tokens can be stolen instantly. While rescueToken patterns are common for recovering stuck tokens, this implementation has no restrictions on which tokens can be rescued, no timelock, and no exclusion of critical tokens (AIS, USDT).
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises admin key; 2. Calls rescueToken(address(AIS_TOKEN), attackerAddr) to steal all AIS tokens meant for user claims; 3. Calls withdrawToTreasury() or rescueToken(address(USDT), attackerAddr) to steal all raised USDT; 4. Users can no longer claim or sell tokens; 5. All user funds are lost in a single transaction
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete loss of all user funds (both contributed USDT and unclaimed AIS tokens). Users who have not yet claimed their tokens lose everything.

matchedCases.matchReason: Admin used rescue/withdraw functions to drain all contract funds without timelock

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Exclude critical tokens from rescue: `require(tokenAddr != address(usdt) && tokenAddr != address(token), 'cannot rescue core tokens');` Apply timelock to fund withdrawals. Consider using a multi-sig for withdrawal operations.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: setToken allows admin to swap token contract without timelock
vulnerabilities.description: The setToken() function allows the owner to instantly replace the AIS token address with any arbitrary ERC20. Users who contributed USDT expecting to receive the original AIS token could instead receive a worthless token when they call claim(). Additionally, the sell() function would then accept the new (potentially worthless) token, while users holding the original token would be unable to sell back. This function has no timelock, no governance approval, and no migration mechanism for existing contributors.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises admin key; 2. Deploys a worthless ERC20 token; 3. Calls setToken(worthlessTokenAddr); 4. When users call claim(), they receive worthless tokens instead of real AIS; 5. Users holding original AIS tokens can no longer sell them back to the contract; 6. All user contributions are effectively stolen
vulnerabilities.impact: Users receive worthless tokens instead of the promised AIS tokens. Existing AIS token holders lose their sell-back guarantee. Complete loss of value for all presale participants.

matchedCases.matchReason: Admin changed token address to redirect claims to worthless token

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Remove setToken() or require governance + 48h timelock. If token migration is needed, implement a two-step process: propose new token → timelock delay → accept new token, with user opt-in for migration.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Spot Price Directly Used as Pricing Basis
vulnerabilities.title: Token price derived from manipulatable spot contract USDT balance
vulnerabilities.description: The _updatePrice() function calculates livePrice as (quoteToken.balanceOf(address(this)) - daoUsdtBalance) / circulatingSupply. This reads the contract's instantaneous token balance directly without any TWAP, oracle, or time-weighted averaging. The balance can be manipulated by: (1) direct USDT transfers to the contract address by anyone, (2) owner changing daoUsdtBalance, or (3) owner withdrawing USDT. All financial operations — buy, sell, dividend claims, referral bonuses, matching rewards — depend on this single manipulatable price value.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker registers as affiliate and buys tokens at price P1; 2. Attacker directly transfers large USDT amount to the contract address (bypassing buy()); 3. Attacker triggers _updatePrice() via any state-changing function (e.g., small buy); 4. Price inflates to P2 >> P1; 5. Attacker sells previously acquired tokens at inflated price P2. Note: the 4x investment sell cap limits direct attacker profit, but the owner or developer (via sellTokenDeveloper with NO sell cap) can extract full value.
vulnerabilities.impact: The entire economic model relies on a price that can be manipulated within a single transaction. While regular users face a 4x sell cap, the developer address (DEVELOPERADDRESS3) can sell unlimited tokens via sellTokenDeveloper() at the manipulated price, enabling full contract drainage. Additionally, direct USDT transfers distort dividend calculations, referral bonus distributions, and matching reward valuations for all users.

matchedCases.matchReason: Price manipulation via manipulating on-chain reserve/balance readings used for valuation
Manipulation of protocol-internal price derived from pool balances

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Replace the balance-based pricing with a Chainlink price feed or a robust TWAP oracle with >30 minute window. If internal pricing is required, implement: (1) a cumulative price observer that tracks balances over time, (2) a maximum price change rate per block (circuit breaker), and (3) separate accounting for user-deposited USDT vs. donated/transferred USDT. Example fix: track deposits only through buy() and maintain an internal reserve variable instead of reading balanceOf.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Owner can arbitrarily set daoUsdtBalance to manipulate token price
vulnerabilities.description: The updateDaoUsdtBalance() function allows the owner to set daoUsdtBalance to any arbitrary value with no timelock, no multi-sig requirement, and no bounds checking. Since _updatePrice() subtracts daoUsdtBalance from the contract's USDT balance to compute the trading reserve, changing this value directly manipulates the token price. Setting daoUsdtBalance to 0 inflates the price; setting it equal to the contract balance crashes the price to MIN_PRICE.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Owner sets daoUsdtBalance = 0, inflating the trading reserve and pushing price to MAX_PRICE; 2. Owner or DEVELOPERADDRESS3 sells tokens at the artificially inflated price via sellTokenDeveloper() (which has no sell cap); 3. Owner restores daoUsdtBalance, or drains remaining USDT via withdrawTokens(). Alternatively: Owner sets daoUsdtBalance very high to crash price, preventing users from selling profitably, then restores it later.
vulnerabilities.impact: The owner has direct, instant control over the token price. This can be used to: prevent user withdrawals (by crashing price), inflate developer token value (by pumping price before developer sells), or manipulate dividend/bonus calculations. All user funds are at risk of owner rug-pull.

matchedCases.matchReason: Privileged role with unrestricted ability to manipulate core economic parameters affecting token price

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add immutable bounds: require(newBalance <= usdtReserve && newBalance >= daoUsdtBalance * 90 / 100). Implement a 48-hour timelock before changes take effect. Require multi-sig approval. Alternatively, make daoUsdtBalance derived from actual DAO deposits rather than a manually set value.

vulnerabilities.patternName: Economic Parameters Adjustable by Privileged Role
vulnerabilities.title: Owner can drain all contract funds including user-deposited USDT
vulnerabilities.description: The withdrawTokens() function allows the owner to withdraw ANY token from the contract, including the quoteToken (USDT) that backs user investments. There is no restriction on which tokens can be withdrawn, no withdrawal limit, and no timelock. Since all user sell operations depend on the contract holding sufficient USDT liquidity, draining the USDT would make it impossible for users to sell their tokens.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Owner calls withdrawTokens(quoteToken, fullBalance); 2. Contract USDT balance goes to 0; 3. All subsequent sell() calls revert with 'Insufficient USDT liquidity in contract'; 4. Price crashes to MIN_PRICE on next _updatePrice() call; 5. Users are left holding worthless tokens with no way to recover their investment.
vulnerabilities.impact: Complete loss of all user funds. The owner can withdraw the entire USDT backing at any time, trapping all user investments. This is a classic rug-pull vector.

matchedCases.matchReason: Owner with unrestricted ability to withdraw liquidity backing user funds

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Restrict withdrawals to non-quote tokens only, or enforce a maximum withdrawal percentage per time period. Add a timelock of at least 48 hours. Track user-deposited USDT separately from protocol-owned USDT and only allow withdrawal of the latter. Example: require(_token != address(quoteToken), 'Cannot withdraw backing asset');

vulnerabilities.patternName: Concentrated Token Mint/Burn Privileges
vulnerabilities.title: Owner can mint unlimited tokens without supply cap
vulnerabilities.description: The mintByOwner() function allows the owner to mint an unlimited number of DLMC tokens to the contract address with no maxSupply cap, no daily limit, and no timelock. While minted tokens initially go to address(this) (not directly increasing circulating supply), the owner can distribute them via batchRegisterAffiliatesWithInvestment() which calls _transfer(address(this), user, holdtoken). Combined with the ability to set arbitrary investment and income values in the same batch function, this enables the owner to create synthetic users with large balances.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Owner calls mintByOwner(largeAmount) to create tokens out of thin air; 2. Owner calls batchRegisterAffiliatesWithInvestment() with holdtoken = largeAmount for a controlled address; 3. That address now holds large token balance; 4. Address sells tokens via sell() or sellTokenDaoMember(), draining the contract's USDT reserves.
vulnerabilities.impact: Unlimited token creation enables the owner to dilute all existing token holders and drain the contract's USDT reserves through newly minted tokens. This is a direct fund extraction vector.

matchedCases.matchReason: Unlimited mint privilege exploited to drain protocol reserves

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add a maxSupply cap. Require governance vote + 48-hour timelock for any mint operation. Track minted amounts and enforce a daily mint limit. Example: require(totalSupply() + amount <= MAX_SUPPLY, 'Exceeds max supply');

vulnerabilities.patternName: No Slippage Protection / Excessive Tolerance
vulnerabilities.title: Buy and sell functions lack slippage protection parameters
vulnerabilities.description: The buy() function does not accept a minTokensOut parameter, and the sell() function does not accept a minUsdtOut parameter. Users cannot specify the minimum acceptable output for their trade. Since the livePrice can change between transaction submission and execution (due to other users' transactions in the same block or direct USDT transfers to the contract), users may receive significantly less than expected.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Victim submits buy(100e6) expecting ~850 tokens at current price 0.1 USDT; 2. Attacker front-runs by directly sending USDT to contract, inflating the price; 3. Alternatively, another buy transaction in the same block increases the price; 4. Victim's transaction executes at the higher price, receiving fewer tokens than expected; 5. Attacker can then sell at the inflated price.
vulnerabilities.impact: Users can be sandwich-attacked or frontrun, receiving fewer tokens on buy or less USDT on sell than expected. The lack of slippage parameters means users have no protection against MEV extraction.

matchedCases.matchReason: Missing slippage protection enabling frontrunning/sandwich attacks

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add minTokensOut parameter to buy() and minUsdtOut parameter to sell(). Example: function buy(uint256 amountQuote, uint256 minTokensOut) external nonReentrant { ... require(tokensToUser >= minTokensOut, 'Slippage exceeded'); }

vulnerabilities.patternName: Missing Deadline / Protection Window
vulnerabilities.title: Buy and sell functions lack deadline parameter for transaction validity window
vulnerabilities.description: Neither buy() nor sell() accepts a deadline parameter. Transactions can be held in the mempool indefinitely and executed at an unfavorable time when the price has significantly changed. Without a deadline, users cannot protect against delayed execution caused by network congestion or malicious MEV operators.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Victim submits a sell transaction when price is favorable; 2. Transaction sits in mempool due to low gas or network congestion; 3. Price changes significantly (via other transactions or owner manipulation); 4. Transaction executes at the unfavorable price, causing the victim to lose value.
vulnerabilities.impact: Users' transactions can be delayed and executed at unfavorable prices. Combined with the lack of slippage protection (VULN-005), this creates a complete absence of MEV protection for all trading operations.

matchedCases.matchReason: Missing deadline parameter allowing delayed execution at unfavorable prices

vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add a deadline parameter to all trading functions. Example: function buy(uint256 amountQuote, uint256 minTokensOut, uint256 deadline) external nonReentrant { require(block.timestamp <= deadline, 'Transaction expired'); ... }

vulnerabilities.patternName: Oracle Address Update Without Timelock/Multi-sig
vulnerabilities.title: Aggregator address can be changed by owner without timelock
vulnerabilities.description: The proposeAggregator() and confirmAggregator() functions allow the owner to redirect the proxy to a new underlying aggregator contract without any timelock delay or multi-signature requirement at the contract level. While a two-step propose/confirm pattern exists, both steps are executable by the same onlyOwner address, meaning they can be called in the same transaction. If the owner key is compromised, an attacker could immediately redirect all price reads to a malicious aggregator that returns arbitrary prices, corrupting every downstream DeFi protocol that depends on this feed. This contract is the official Chainlink proxy design and is operationally mitigated by Chainlink's multi-sig wallet infrastructure, but the contract code itself enforces no timelock or multi-sig requirement.
vulnerabilities.attackVector: 1. Attacker compromises the owner key (single EOA or multi-sig quorum breach); 2. Call proposeAggregator(maliciousAggregator) to set the proposed aggregator; 3. Call confirmAggregator(maliciousAggregator) in the same transaction to activate it; 4. The malicious aggregator returns inflated/deflated prices; 5. Downstream protocols (lending, DEX, perps) read corrupted prices from this proxy; 6. Attacker exploits the price discrepancy in downstream protocols to extract funds. Steps 2-3 can be atomic in a single transaction, giving consumers no window to react.
vulnerabilities.impact: All downstream DeFi protocols consuming this oracle feed would receive corrupted prices. In a lending protocol, this enables unfair liquidations or over-borrowing. In a DEX or perp, it enables arbitrary price exploitation. The blast radius is catastrophic since a single Chainlink proxy feed (e.g., ETH/USD) may be consumed by dozens of protocols holding billions in TVL.

matchedCases.caseName: Chainlink Oracle Considerations (multiple DeFi exploits using stale/manipulated feeds)
matchedCases.matchReason: Oracle redirection or compromise leading to cascading DeFi exploitation; though no direct Chainlink proxy compromise has occurred, the architectural risk is identical to centralized oracle attack vectors seen in other protocols

vulnerabilities.recommendation: This is the official Chainlink proxy design and is operationally secured by Chainlink's multi-sig infrastructure. For maximum defense-in-depth at the contract level: (1) Add a timelock to aggregator changes so consumers can monitor and react to proposed changes, e.g., require 48 hours between proposeAggregator and confirmAggregator; (2) Enforce multi-sig at the contract level using a Gnosis Safe or similar multi-signature pattern instead of relying solely on operational security; (3) Downstream consumers should implement their own staleness checks (block.timestamp - updatedAt < heartbeat) and deviation circuit breakers, and should monitor aggregator proposal events for early warning. Example timelock addition: store proposedAggregator with a proposedTimestamp, and in confirmAggregator require(block.timestamp >= proposedTimestamp + 48 hours).
